title: Scenario Variations locate a rule's boundary by substituting facts until the finding flips
content:
A.1.2.2.2.29 defines Scenario Variations: documents nested under an original Scenario, addressed by appending 'var' and a number (`A.1.1.0.4.1.1.1.var2`). Each "substitutes elements of its original Scenario to demonstrate whether and why the finding of Aligned/Misaligned would change."

This is a deliberately different epistemic act from writing another Scenario. A second independent Scenario adds another data point; a Variation performs a **controlled experiment** — hold the fact pattern fixed, change one element, observe whether the verdict moves. That isolates which facts are actually doing the work in a rule and which are incidental colour.

The practical value shows up at the edge cases, which is where adjudication actually happens. A facilitator facing a novel situation does not need a scenario that matches it; they need to know which features of a scenario are dispositive, so they can tell whether their situation is on the same side of the line. A family of Variations around one Scenario answers that directly.

It is also a check on the Tenet itself. If varying a fact that the Tenet's stated logic says should matter does *not* change the finding — or vice versa — the Tenet is mis-stated. Variations make Tenets falsifiable against their own worked examples, which is a stronger property than mere illustration.
description: Each Variation (suffix 'varN') changes elements of its parent Scenario to demonstrate whether and why the Aligned/Misaligned finding would change — mapping the edge, not the centre.
